towels.title: Custom Golf Towels: A Practical Procurement Guide
towels.imageAlt: ZHONI golf towel and branding concepts for product development
intro: Choose custom golf towels by deciding how golfers will use and carry them, then align the fabric, attachment and branding with that use. For a towel that stays connected to a bag loop, start by discussing a clip-attached format. For frequent removal and replacement, consider a magnetic direction and identify the actual contact point.
The best brief connects those decisions. A larger logo, heavier towel or different attachment can change how the finished product hangs, handles and packs.

sections.title: Choose the attachment around the handling

rows: Towel remains connected to a bag during use
Clip or carabiner attachment
Connection location, reach and ease of removal
Towel is repeatedly removed and replaced
Magnetic attachment
Suitable contact point and attachment behaviour
Towel is presented inside a player pack
Either, according to intended use
Folded size, visible logo and hardware protection

after: A magnetic attachment is not compatible with every cart surface or bag component. Identify the proposed contact point before choosing the assembly; assess the finished towel there, including when wet.
For ZHONI’s custom towel range, attachment is a useful first discussion—not an accessory decision left until after the artwork is finished.

sections.title: Compare fabric beyond the material name
paragraphs: Microfiber waffle and cotton are useful directions to compare, but neither name defines the complete towel.

Ask for composition, finished dimensions, fabric weight and edging. Then compare samples for the cleaning feel, folded bulk and decoration you want. If drying behaviour or absorbency is a purchasing requirement, agree how it will be assessed rather than inferring a result from the word ‘microfiber’.
Choose the towel format before increasing logo size. Branding should remain visible without unnecessarily occupying the area intended for cleaning.

sections.title: A practical example: visible branding without a full-face logo
paragraphs: Consider an illustrative club-shop brief: a dark towel with a small light-coloured emblem, intended to hang from a golf bag.

The buyer wants the emblem visible while preserving a substantial cleaning area. Rather than enlarging the artwork across the towel, first compare the hanging fold and attachment position. Place the proposed emblem on the exposed section, then inspect the reverse of the embroidery and the open towel.
This turns ‘make the logo more visible’ into a placement decision rather than automatically adding more decoration.

sections.title: What should a comparable quotation include?
paragraphs: Align the towel dimensions, composition or fabric reference, colour quantities, attachment, logo size and packing.

Ask whether decoration setup, samples, hardware and freight are included. A loose clip-attached towel and a boxed magnetic towel are different quotations, even when both are described as ‘custom golf towels’.
If specifications are unfinished, send ZHONI a product reference and the changes you want. Final fabric weight or hardware details do not need to be settled before the first discussion.

sections.title: What should the sample resolve?
paragraphs: Review the towel open and hanging. Check the useful cleaning area, edge stitching, logo appearance and reverse-side finish.

Try the proposed attachment at its intended contact point. Where washing behaviour matters, agree a review method and acceptance criteria for the relevant concerns, such as colour transfer, shrinkage or attachment security.
The sample should answer the uncertainties in your brief—not simply confirm that the logo exists.

sections.title: Packing, MOQ and delivery planning
paragraphs: Choose packing around the product’s role. A band or protective bag may suit a standalone towel; a presentation box adds a separate specification and assembly requirement.
Confirm the folded dimensions and protect neighbouring items from exposed hardware. Use the packed product dimensions when discussing freight.

Custom colours, quantity per design, decoration setup, attachment sourcing and packing can change MOQ and scheduling. Work back from the required receipt date, allowing for approvals, production, inspection, transport and destination handling.

faqs: Can I order towels without a complete gift set?
Yes. ZHONI’s product focus includes standalone custom golf towels. Supporting products and gift packaging are optional parts of the discussion.
What if I do not know whether magnetic or clip attachment is better?
Share where the towel should connect and whether golfers should remove it frequently. Those details are more useful initially than choosing hardware from a photograph.
What information is enough to start?
A reference, logo and intended use. Add approximate quantity, destination and required receipt date when available.

close.title: Discuss your towel direction
paragraphs: Share your reference and desired changes. Tell ZHONI how the towel should hang and what the golfer should see when it is in use.

caps.title: Custom Golf Caps and Visors: A Buyer’s Guide
caps.imageAlt: ZHONI cap, rope cap, visor and bucket hat design concepts
intro: Choose custom golf caps by matching the intended wearer and brand presentation to the cap’s shape, then review fabric, fit and logo application together. Start with a supported crown when a defined front shape is important; explore an unstructured crown when a softer silhouette is the priority. Choose a visor when an open crown is specifically wanted.
A reference cap can start the discussion. Explain which features you want to retain and which should change.

sections.title: Choose a silhouette before a decoration method

rows: Structured cap
A defined front profile is central to the look
Crown support and depth must suit the wearer
Unstructured cap
A soft, relaxed silhouette is preferred
Logo scale and decoration must work with the softer front
Rope or five-panel direction
Panel layout or rope detail is part of the identity
Seams and front proportions affect artwork placement
Visor
An open crown is wanted
Band depth, adjustment and branding area differ from a cap
Bucket hat
A surrounding brim is part of the brief
Fit and logo presentation require a separate construction review

after: For a collection combining several styles, coordinate colour and logo hierarchy rather than forcing identical artwork dimensions onto every product.

sections.title: Choose fabric as part of the whole cap
paragraphs: Cotton twill is a useful direction when the buyer wants a familiar woven texture. Polyester constructions are worth discussing when the brief prioritises active-use fabric requirements. Mesh-back constructions introduce a different rear-panel structure and appearance.

Compare actual fabric references alongside crown support, sweatband and closure. Do not treat ‘performance’ as a complete specification: quick-drying, UV-protection and water-repellent claims each need an applicable basis.

sections.title: Resolve the logo before committing to its size
paragraphs: A front emblem, fine lettering and a large patch create different branding questions. Assess the actual artwork at the proposed size, including panel seams and the support behind the decoration.
Illustrative brief: a club likes a low-profile, unstructured cap but wants an emblem containing small text.

There are several directions to discuss: retain the full emblem and reconsider its scale, use an authorised simplified mark, or explore a different placement or application. Enlarging the logo is not automatically the best answer if it changes the understated appearance the buyer liked.
ZHONI’s cap discussion can begin with that precise conflict: the shape to preserve and the branding detail that must remain readable.

sections.title: Compare quotations on the same construction
paragraphs: Include the cap or visor style, fabric reference, crown profile, colour quantities, wearer-size direction and closure. Identify artwork for each placement, plus any labels, hangtags or packing.
Separate decoration setup, patches, labels and presentation packaging where relevant. Two caps with the same front logo can still differ substantially in construction and included finishing.
You do not need a finished technical pack to approach ZHONI. A reference with ‘keep this shape, change this logo and closure’ is a useful first brief.

sections.title: Use the sample to review wear, not just appearance
paragraphs: Try crown depth, brim shape, adjustment and closure comfort on the intended wearer group. Review the sweatband and interior finishing as well as the front logo.
An adjustable closure does not establish universal fit. Likewise, a flat artwork approval cannot confirm how embroidery looks across the finished crown.
Record the agreed sample and relevant measurements as the production reference.

sections.title: Pack for the agreed shape and plan for receipt
paragraphs: Specify whether caps will be nested or individually presented. Review crown and brim protection, labels and carton dimensions. When presentation is important, inspect a packed sample after unpacking.

MOQ and timing can change with fabric availability, custom colours, quantity per style, size allocation, branding and labels. Include fit revisions and artwork approval before bulk production, then allow for packing and delivery to the destination.

faqs: Should a tournament choose caps or visors?
Choose around the intended wearer group and preferred construction. A cap and visor can share a visual identity, but they need separate fit and branding decisions.
Can I keep a reference shape and use my own logo?
That is a useful starting brief. Explain the silhouette features you want to retain and use artwork you are authorised to reproduce.
Can caps be ordered as the main product?
Yes. ZHONI focuses on custom caps and visors as a core product category; a wider gift set is not a prerequisite.

close.title: Bring the shape and the change
paragraphs: Send the reference, your logo and the most important change first; add quantities and timing when known.

plush.title: Custom Plush Golf Headcovers: From Character to a Practical Design Brief
plush.imageAlt: Illustrative ZHONI bear, bird and geometric plush golf headcover concepts
intro: Start a custom plush golf headcover with two references: the character you want people to recognise and the club the cover is intended to fit. Rank the character’s essential features, then develop the outer form, lining and opening around those priorities.
A mascot drawing can communicate the identity. It does not, by itself, determine the three-dimensional construction or club fit.

sections.title: Preserve the identity, not every drawn detail
paragraphs: List the features that make the character recognisable: its silhouette, face proportions, colour blocks or distinctive ears, beak or crest.
Then separate essential features from details that may change. This gives development a clear priority when a flat drawing must become panels, seams and dimensional parts.
Provide front, side and rear views where available. If only one view exists, identify what remains undecided rather than letting the unseen back or underside become an accidental design choice.
Use original artwork or references you are authorised to develop.

sections.title: Balance character detail with the club opening
paragraphs: Consider an illustrative animal-headcover brief with long ears and a narrow neck.

The ears may be essential to recognition, while the narrow neck creates questions about the opening. Instead of treating the illustration as a fixed cutting pattern, first identify which proportions can change and what space the intended club requires.
This is a useful conversation to bring to ZHONI: ‘Keep the ear silhouette and face, but explore the lower form around this club reference.’
It establishes what the character must communicate without pretending that the construction has already been solved.

sections.title: Choose each material for its role

rows: Outer plush
Character texture and visual detail
Pile direction, face readability and decoration
Supporting construction
Intended dimensional form
How projecting or shaped features are supported
Lining
Interior contact and coverage
Coverage, seams and interaction with the opening
Opening and retention
Insertion, removal and position on the club
Actual target club and finished sample behaviour

after: Shorter pile can be a direction to explore when fine facial detail is a priority; longer pile creates a different textured appearance. Review the actual material and decoration together rather than choosing from a fabric name alone.

sections.title: Make branding support the character
paragraphs: Decide whether the character itself carries the identity or whether an additional logo is needed.

A large emblem placed over the face may compete with the feature buyers are paying to recognise. A secondary placement may be worth exploring when the character should lead. The available area and decoration method still depend on the selected construction.
For several character versions, review what can genuinely be shared. Similar club openings do not automatically mean identical patterns, especially when heads, ears or proportions change.

sections.title: Quote the development scope, not just the unit
paragraphs: Share authorised character views, essential features, target club, quantity per character or fit variant, and packing requirements.

Ask how pattern development, decoration setup, sample revisions and bulk units are treated. A new dimensional character and a minor variation of an agreed construction are different development briefs.
For an initial discussion, send the character reference and target club first. Finished panel drawings are not required to explain the idea.

sections.title: What must a physical sample answer?
paragraphs: Review recognition from several angles, proportions, seam placement and attached details. Fit the sample to the intended club and assess insertion, removal, lining coverage and retention.
A rendering can help agree visual direction. It cannot verify physical fit, protection or durability.

Consolidate sample comments into one approval record so a change to the face does not obscure an unresolved opening issue. Where safety or durability assessment is needed, define that requirement before ordering.

sections.title: Treat packing as a design decision
paragraphs: Projecting ears, crests or other features may affect the packed volume and presentation after unpacking.

Review protection, support and carton fill around the finished sample. Assess whether the character returns to the agreed form after unpacking before choosing a packing method solely to reduce freight volume.

Pattern development, material availability, character variants and revision rounds also affect timing. Keep sample development separate from bulk production, and plan against destination receipt rather than dispatch alone.

faqs: Can a flat mascot become a plush golf headcover?
It can provide the starting reference. The design still needs interpretation into volume, seams, materials and an opening around the intended club.
Can several characters share one construction?
Possibly, where volume and opening requirements align. Significant changes to proportions or projecting features may require separate patterns and sample review.
What should I send if the artwork is unfinished?
Send the authorised reference, target club and features that must remain recognisable. Identify the parts still open for discussion.

close.title: Start with the identity and the intended club
paragraphs: ZHONI focuses on custom plush headcovers alongside golf towels and caps. For a character project, the useful first decision is what must stay recognisable and what can change to accommodate the club.
